items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: P less than 0.05 doesn't mean a result is true — or even probably true
items.claim: A study finds an effect with p = 0.04. Headlines say 'statistically significant'. The reader assumes the effect is real. In fact, in some scientific fields, more than half of 'p < 0.05' findings fail to replicate.

options.text: The probability the effect is real is 96%

The probability of seeing data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true is 4%. Says nothing directly about the probability the effect is real, which requires Bayesian reasoning with priors
The result is wrong 4% of the time
P-values measure the size of effects

items.reveal_title: P-value misinterpretation and the replication crisis
items.reveal:
P-value definition: P(data at least as extreme as observed | null hypothesis true).

Common misinterpretations:
1. P is the probability the null is true (no).
2. (1 - p) is the probability the effect is real (no).
3. P measures effect size (no — small effects in large studies can have tiny p).
4. P < 0.05 means 'real effect' (no — depends on prior plausibility and study design).

Replication crisis (2010s): many influential findings in psychology, biomedicine, economics fail to replicate.
- Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies. ~36% of replications succeeded (vs ~97% of original studies reporting significance).
- Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (2021) attempted 23 cancer findings; only 25% of effects were as strong in replication.
- Many famous psychology results (ego depletion, power posing, money priming) have not replicated.

Causes:
- P-hacking (running many tests, reporting only significant ones).
- Publication bias (significant findings published; null results filed away).
- Small samples + multiple testing.
- Garden of forking paths (each analytic choice creates uncounted tests).
- Underpowered studies (true effects mixed with noise; significant results when found are overestimates).

Reforms: preregistration, registered reports, focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals, replication studies, statistical training reform, banishing the 0.05 threshold (some journals).

Bayesian alternatives: P(hypothesis | data) directly. Requires explicit priors but gives more interpretable answers.

The ASA's 2016 statement on p-values: don't use 'p < 0.05' as the sole basis for conclusions. Distance is being made from this old standard.
items.why: P-values look like simple measures of certainty. They aren't. Misinterpreting them has contributed to a massive scientific replication crisis. Understanding what p-values do and don't say is essential to reading research.

items.title: There are true statements about numbers that cannot be proved
items.claim: Hilbert (1900) hoped to put mathematics on a complete, consistent axiomatic foundation. In 1931, Kurt Gödel proved it impossible. Any system of axioms expressive enough to do basic arithmetic contains true statements that the system cannot prove.
items.prompt: What's the heart of Gödel's argument?

options.text: Gödel constructed a self-referential statement G: 'G cannot be proved within this system'. If the system could prove G, the system would prove something false (contradiction). If the system can't prove G, then G is true and unprovable

items.reveal:
Gödel encoded statements about mathematics AS numbers (Gödel numbering), so the system could 'talk about itself'. He then constructed a sentence asserting its own unprovability.

First incompleteness theorem: any consistent system strong enough to express arithmetic contains a true statement it cannot prove.
Second incompleteness theorem: such a system cannot prove its own consistency from within itself.

The results devastated Hilbert's program. They also bounded what computers can do: the halting problem (Turing 1936) is undecidable in essentially the same way.

Gödel was 25 when he proved it. Hilbert took it badly. Gödel later starved himself to death (1978) — convinced his food was being poisoned, he stopped eating when his wife was hospitalised.

Mathematics is still consistent (presumably), still useful, still extending — just provably incomplete.
items.why: Mathematics is treated as a closed, fully derivable system. Gödel showed any rich enough system has fundamental gaps — true things it can never prove.
